data.title: Middle East Eye: Netanyahu calls for unity government without 'Hamas supporters'
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Netanyahu calls for unity government without 'Hamas supporters'
In a video statement released on Monday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said forming a unity government was an "absolute necessity".
"Two days ago I called for the formation of a unity government, and this is the need of the hour," Netanyahu said.
"You cannot form a government with Hamas supporters," he added. "You cannot fight Iran and the rest of its followers within extremist Islam if, inside the government, you rely on supporters of extremist Islam."
Netanyahu said the government should include all parties of the national camp, including Haredi parties, as well as the other Zionist parties, and should be led by Likud.
"It is only natural that the largest party should lead this government," he said.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for a Likud-led unity government, describing it as an “absolute necessity”. He insisted it should include Haredi and other Zionist parties while excluding those he labelled “Hamas supporters”. https://t.co/sI4LzFphLz

data.title: Middle East Eye: Senior UAE official says Gulf faces 'prolonged uncertainty' with no settlement to Iran war
data.author: Hossam Desouky
data.summary:
Senior UAE official says Gulf faces 'prolonged uncertainty' with no settlement to Iran war
A senior UAE official warned that the Gulf must be prepared for a “long period of uncertainty” in which the US and Iran are not able to come to a political settlement to end their war, leaving the region in a state of limbo.
"We should... prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional order can be taken for granted,” Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic advisor to UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed, said on Monday at a forum in Abu Dhabi.
Gargash’s remarks come as the Middle East tries to decipher whether US President Donald Trump will launch fresh strikes on Iran.
Expectations of a new attack were high until last week, when on 3 November the Democrats won a sweeping midterm election victory that Trump and Vice President JD Vance attributed to the unpopularity of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Trump told CNN on Monday it was “highly unlikely” he would attack while negotiations are ongoing.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Nearly 80 percent of Britons see Israel as a threat to world peace
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Nearly 80 percent of Britons see Israel as a threat to world peace
Nearly four in five Britons see Israel as a serious threat to world peace, according to a survey published last week by the National Centre for Social Research (NatCen).
The figure rose from 48 percent in 2005 to 78 percent this spring, two-and-a-half years into the genocide in Gaza and just after Israel and the US had attacked Iran.
In July, a YouGov opinion poll commissioned by the Council for British-Arab Understanding found that only 17 percent of the British population believes that Israel is not committing genocide in Gaza.
The war on Iran has hit the UK economy, leaving households paying more for energy, food and mortgages. The rising bills have brought the cost of Israel’s wars in the Middle East home to British households.
Last week, the Bank of England raised its base rate from 3.75 percent to 4 percent, its first increase in more than three years. The rise pushes up payments for borrowers on mortgages and adds to the cost of taking out or renewing a home loan.

data.title: Middle East Eye: The Arab vote in the Israeli elections
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
The Arab vote in the Israeli elections
Two weeks after Israel held its first general elections since October 2023, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been tasked with forming a government.
The election saw a historic voter turnout for Palestinian citizens of Israel, who headed to the ballot for one reason: to oust Benjamin Netanyahu.
On this One on One, Balad party leader Sami Abou Shehadeh tells Middle East Eye that although the Arab vote has prevented Netanyahu from forming another far-right government, racism against Palestinians is still prevalent across the Israeli political board.
"The current situation for the Palestinian minority in Israel, we do not have good options. We are choosing between bad and worse," he tells MEE, warning that Netanyahu is "in a very dangerous phase" as he doubles down his efforts to delegitimise the election results and push for a repeat election.
